title: Definition, risk factors and sided distribution
guide: Infection of the valvular/endocardial surface involving native or prosthetic valves and intracardiac devices, leading to vegetations (the hallmark); risk factors: congenital (VSD, ASD), rheumatic (mitral and aortic regurgitation, no risk with mitral stenosis), degenerative calcific aortic stenosis and IV drug abuse; distribution: left sided most common (aortic valve, MVP with MR), combined 15%, right sided 10% of which 70% is MRSA, tricuspid, seen in IV drug abusers and IV central lines.

title: Pathogenesis, classification and organisms
guide: Mucosal injury → bacterial seeding; valvular endothelial injury → platelet-fibrin clot = NBTE (non-bacterial thrombotic, marantic endocarditis, also seen in SLE with catheters) → bacterial adherence → proliferation → vegetation → endocarditic features; classified as native valve, prosthetic valve, IVDA and health-care associated; native valve most often mitral (left sided), with MVP + MR, VSD and CKD-associated tricuspid disease; predisposing conditions with percentages: rheumatic 25-30, congenital 10-20, MVP 10-30, degenerative rare, parenteral drug abuse 15-35, none 25-45; organisms: native valve S. aureus > Strep. viridans > enterococci; prosthetic < 12 months CoNS > MRSA > Gram-negative bacilli; > 12 months Strep. viridans > S. aureus > enterococci; IV drug use MRSA; acute IE has about 60% mortality with abscess, osteomyelitis, severe sepsis and destroyed valves, managed as sepsis.

title: Subacute infective endocarditis
guide: Background of congenital heart disease with childhood rheumatic fever treated as RHD; symptoms: fever with chills for 2-3 months, anorexia, weight loss, fatigue, myalgia; signs: new or worsening murmur, macroembolic events (stroke, ACS, retinal occlusion), microembolic events (petechiae, splinter haemorrhages), splenomegaly/clubbing, arterial embolisation; vasculitic manifestations: Osler nodes, rheumatoid factor, Roth spots (retinal endothelial vasculitis, pale centre with surrounding erythema); laboratory: normocytic anaemia, raised WBC, ESR and CRP, rheumatoid factor positive in 50% and proteinuria with microscopic haematuria in 50%; Janeway lesions (soles, palms, thenar/hypothenar, plantar toes; variable irregular macules; non-tender; days-weeks; acute; culture positive; septic microemboli) versus Osler nodes (finger/toe tips and pulps; 1 mm to >1 cm nodules; tender; hours-days; subacute; culture negative; vasculitis).

title: Complications and the modified Duke criteria
guide: Causes of the immune complex picture: IE with low C3 and C4, hepatitis C, cryoglobulinaemia and leprosy; cardiac complications: stroke/ACS from fragment embolisation into coronaries, heart failure from valvular insufficiency with new adult AR/MR, perivalvular abscess (common in the aortic position) causing conduction block; non-cardiac: embolic occlusion, immunological, metastatic infection and mycotic aneurysm; right-sided IE: pulmonary abscess, empyema, right heart failure and mycotic aneurysm of the pulmonary artery; modified Duke criteria: 2 major, or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor; major blood-culture criteria: 3 sets of 20 ml from 3 sites, 10 ml aerobic plus 10 ml anaerobic per bottle taken over 30-60 minutes and repeated every 18-24 hours, with typical organisms (MRSA, Strep. viridans) from two separate cultures, persistently positive cultures, or a single positive culture/antibodies for HACEK group or Coxiella burnetii.

title: Minor criteria and echocardiography
guide: Minor criteria: predisposition, fever, vascular phenomenon (emboli), immunological phenomenon and microbiological evidence not meeting culture criteria; TTE sensitivity 50-70% with 86% specificity, TEE sensitivity 86-98% with 98% specificity; suspected endocarditis with a native valve goes to TTE while prosthetic valves and intracardiac devices go to TEE; positive echo means treat for endocarditis, negative means observe and repeat echo if required, TEE is added when complications are suspected; TEE is preferred over TTE for vegetations under 2 mm, myocardial abscess, valve perforation, prosthetic valve, CIED and intracardiac fistula.

title: Treatment, surgery and prophylaxis
guide: Strep. viridans: penicillin G 2-3 million units IV q4h for 4 weeks, else ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily or vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV BD, with vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV BD for 4-6 weeks if penicillin resistant; enterococci: penicillin G 4-5 million units q4h for 4-6 weeks with gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV TDS, vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV BD if penicillin resistant; enterococci and Listeria are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; MRSA: vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV BD for 4-6 weeks in native valves, plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV BD and rifampicin 300 mg oral TID for 6-8 weeks in prosthetic valves; culture-report-negative disease is common, follows antibiotics and is treated with ceftriaxone plus gentamicin, whereas true culture-negative disease is rare, follows no antibiotics and is treated with vancomycin plus gentamicin for 4-6 weeks; surgery for native valves with acute regurgitation, fungal endocarditis or perivalvular aortic abscess and for prosthetic valves with dehiscence, increasing obstruction/regurgitation or heart failure; prophylaxis for prosthetic valves, previous IE, post-cardiac transplant, unrepaired CHD and repaired CHD within 6 months, before dental procedures and invasive respiratory-tract procedures (adenoidectomy, tonsillectomy, incision and drainage of respiratory mucosa), with amoxicillin 2 g orally 30-60 minutes before, azithromycin 500 mg, cephalexin 2 g or clindamycin 600 mg in penicillin allergy, ampicillin 2 g IV or ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM if unable to take orally, and clindamycin 600 mg IV for allergy plus parenteral need.
